title: Secure Access with Microsoft Entra ID
_note: One file per module. 'sub_skill' must quote a verbatim sub-objective from the module's front matter, so a wrong answer names what to re-read. 'answer' is a zero-based index, or an array of indexes for multiple response.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure managed identities for Azure resources
questions.prompt: An application running on several virtual machines must read secrets from Key Vault. The security team requires that no credential exists in code or configuration, and that the same identity survives if any individual VM is rebuilt. What should you configure?
options: A system-assigned managed identity on each virtual machine
A user-assigned managed identity attached to each virtual machine
An app registration with a client secret stored in Key Vault
An app registration with a certificate deployed to each virtual machine
questions.explanation: A user-assigned identity is a standalone Azure resource, shareable across resources and surviving their deletion. A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource and deleted with it, so it fails the second requirement. Both app registration options reintroduce a credential.
why_not: A system-assigned identity is tied to one VM and deleted with it, so a rebuilt VM gets a different identity - it fails the second requirement.
An app registration with a client secret reintroduces a credential. Storing it in Key Vault moves the secret; it does not remove it.
A certificate is still a credential, now deployed to every VM - it fails the first requirement.

questions.prompt: Policy A requires multifactor authentication. Policy B requires a compliant device. Policy C blocks sign-ins from a named country. A user in scope of all three signs in from that country, with MFA satisfied and a compliant device. What is the outcome?
options: Access is granted, because the grant controls in A and B were satisfied
Access is granted, because policy priority favours the lower-numbered policy
Access is blocked, because block takes precedence over grant
Access is granted only for the session duration configured in policy C
questions.explanation: Every applicable policy is evaluated on every sign-in and there is no priority ordering. If any applicable policy blocks, the sign-in is blocked regardless of how many others would have granted.
why_not: Satisfying A and B does not matter: policy C also applies, and block wins over any number of grants.
Conditional Access has no priority ordering. Every enabled policy that applies is evaluated on every sign-in.
Policy C's control is Block, which denies the sign-in outright. Session controls only shape access that has been granted.

questions.sub_skill: Manage OAuth permission grants and consent settings
questions.prompt: Two applications each hold the Microsoft Graph permission Mail.Read. Application A holds it as a delegated permission; application B holds it as an application permission. A user with access to one mailbox signs in to application A. Which statements are true?
options: Application A can read only that user's mailbox
Application A can read every mailbox in the tenant
Application B can read every mailbox in the tenant
Application B requires admin consent
questions.explanation: Delegated permissions give the intersection of the grant and the signed-in user's own access. Application permissions have no user to intersect with, so the scope is tenant-wide, and they always require admin consent. The permission name is identical in both cases.
why_not: Delegated permissions are capped by the signed-in user's own access - the intersection of the grant and what the user can reach - so A sees only that one mailbox.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure authentication methods, including multifactor authentication (MFA) and passwordless
questions.prompt: A requirement states that administrators must authenticate with a passkey or certificate, and that SMS must not be accepted. Which Conditional Access grant control satisfies this?
options: Require multifactor authentication
Require authentication strength, set to phishing-resistant MFA
Require compliant device
Require approved client app
questions.explanation: The generic MFA control accepts any registered method, including SMS. An authentication strength names the acceptable method combinations, which is how the requirement is expressed as policy rather than as guidance.
why_not: Require multifactor authentication accepts any registered method, including SMS.
A compliant device is a device requirement. It says nothing about which authentication methods are acceptable.
Approved client app restricts which client applications can be used, not how the user authenticates.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure identity for applications, including enterprise applications and app registrations
questions.prompt: You delete an app registration from your tenant for a multi-tenant application that several partner organisations had consented to. What happens to the service principals in the partner tenants?
options: They are deleted automatically, because the application object was the parent
They remain, because each tenant holds its own service principal and consent grants
They are disabled but retained for 30 days in each partner tenant
They are converted to single-tenant app registrations in each partner tenant
questions.explanation: The app registration is the definition and exists once, in the home tenant. Each consenting tenant holds its own service principal with its own grants, and those are not removed by deleting the registration.
why_not: The application object exists once, in the home tenant. Each partner tenant's service principal is its own object and is not removed with it.
Deleting the home-tenant registration does not reach into partner tenants, so there is no disable-and-retain step there. Their service principals remain until each tenant removes its own.
A service principal cannot become an app registration. They are different object types, and the registration exists only in the home tenant.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
questions.prompt: Five engineers need the Security Administrator role. Requirements: nobody holds the role until they need it; every use must be approved by a second person and record a justification; and the role must lapse four hours after it is activated. What should you configure?
options: An active assignment for each engineer that expires after four hours
An eligible assignment for each engineer, with the Security Administrator role settings requiring approval, justification, and a four-hour maximum activation duration
An eligible assignment for each engineer, with approval and justification set on each individual assignment
A permanent active assignment for each engineer, plus a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for users holding the Security Administrator role
questions.explanation: Eligibility removes standing access: the engineers hold nothing until they activate. Approval, justification and maximum activation duration are settings of the role - its role management policy - and apply to every activation of that role. The eligible assignment is only the roster; the role settings are the control.
why_not: An active assignment is held from the moment it starts, with no request, no approval and no justification. Expiring it after four hours bounds the assignment, not each use of the role.

Approval, justification and maximum activation duration are not properties of an individual assignment. They are role settings; an assignment carries only its start and end dates and whether it is eligible or active.
The engineers still hold the role permanently. Conditional Access adds a sign-in requirement but gives you no approval, no justification and no time limit.
questions.misconception: Approval and activation rules are set on each assignment
